claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robinow and White, 1988.

claims.claim: Neuron-specific knockdown of DCP1 in D. melanogaster resulted in a significant reduction of lifespan.
claims.source: The subsequent neuron-specific knockdown of DCP1, verified by qRT-PCR (Figure 5A), resulted in a significant reduction of lifespan, as elav:GAL4 >UAS:IRDCP1 progeny of either UAS:IRDCP1 strain were extremely short-lived compared to their parental elav:GAL4 flies at 25°C, and at 29°C where UAS/GAL4 system is most effective (Figure 5B, C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A and lifespan data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: elav:GAL4 >UAS:DCP1:eGFP flies grown at 25°C or 29°C did not live longer than their parental elav:GAL4 strain.
claims.source: In contrast to our expectations, elav:GAL4 >UAS:DCP1:eGFP flies grown at 25°C or 29°C did not live longer than their parental elav:GAL4 strain (Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data referenced in Figure 5—source data 1.

claims.claim: elav:GAL4 >UAS:DCP1:eGFP;GAL80ts flies that overexpress neuronal DCP1 post-developmentally exhibited a significant increase of both median (~42%) and maximum (~27%) lifespan compared to their parental elav:GAL4 strain.
claims.source: Interestingly, these flies that overexpress neuronal DCP1 post-developmentally exhibited a significant increase of both median (~42%) and maximum (~27%) lifespan compared to their parental elav:GAL4 strain (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: High levels of DCP1 in neurons (or neuron precursors) are detrimental during development, but have an opposing lifespan-extending effect during adulthood.
claims.source: Thus, high levels of DCP1 in neurons (or neuron precursors) are detrimental during development, but have an opposing lifespan-extending effect during adulthood.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the developmental and post-developmental DCP1 overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: Neuronal DCP1 knockdown causes malformed/unexpanded wings in ~50% of the population at 25°C.
claims.source: While studying elav:GAL4 >UAS:IRDCP1 flies we noticed that neuronal DCP1 knockdown causes a characteristic phenotype, defined by malformed/unexpanded wings (Figure 5E) in ~50% of the population at 25°C (n = 178 for GD31442 and n = 244 for KK105638).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The penetrance of wing malformations from neuronal DCP1 knockdown reached a remarkable 95% at 29°C.
claims.source: This effect did not correlate with the efficiency of the knockdown, since all flies exhibited the same levels of DCP1 mRNA regardless of their wing phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), neither with their lifespan, which was short in all cases. Nonetheless, penetrance reached a remarkable 95% at 29°C (n = 167).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations at 29°C.

claims.claim: Wing malformations from neuronal DCP1 knockdown always coincided with the presence of additional morphological aberrations, which include an unexpanded thorax and the lack of cuticle tanning.
claims.source: Notably, wing malformations always coincided with the presence of additional morphological aberrations, which include an unexpanded thorax (judged by the crossing of postscutellar bristles) and the lack of cuticle tanning (melanisation and hardening) (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: mRNA decapping in the nervous system can affect development in non-neuronal cells of D. melanogaster.
claims.source: Such defects indicate that mRNA decapping in the nervous system can affect development in non-neuronal cells of D. melanogaster.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the morphological defects observed in neuronal DCP1 knockdown flies.

claims.claim: 15 out of 23 isolated wing imaginal discs from larvae with neuronal DCP1 knockdown exhibited widespread structural anomalies, associated with abnormal epithelial folding.
claims.source: Despite the neuronal DCP1 knockdown, 15 out of 23 isolated discs exhibited widespread structural anomalies, associated with abnormal epithelial folding, which were absent in discs from age-matched larvae of parental UAS:IRDCP1 and elav:GAL4 strains (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: elav:GAL4-driven GFP fluorescence was observed in the majority of neuronal brain cells but no fluorescent signal was detected in wing imaginal discs.
claims.source: To rule out any leakage in the specificity of our system that could lead to DCP1 knockdown in wing disc epithelial cells and affect their morphology cell autonomously (Casas-Tintó et al., 2017), we monitored elav:GAL4-driven GFP fluorescence in tissues derived from elav:GAL4 >UAS:DCP1:eGFP third instar larvae. As expected we observed strong fluorescence in the majority of neuronal brain cells but we detected no fluorescent signal in wing imaginal discs (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Using an en:GAL4 driver to knock down DCP1 expression only in the posterior part of the wing disc did not result in any structural differences between the anterior and the posterior part of en:GAL4 >UAS:IRDCP1 wing discs.
claims.source: Additionally, we used an en:GAL4 driver to examine the effect of DCP1 deficiency in wing disc epithelial cells by knocking down its expression only in the posterior part of the disc. This did not result in any structural differences between the anterior and the posterior part of en:GAL4 >UAS:IRDCP1 wing discs, both of which had normal morphology in 12 out of 13 examined wing imaginal discs (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Neuronal DCP1 is implicated in a cell non-autonomous mechanism that uses neuronally derived signals to orchestrate wing disc development.
claims.source: These results implicate neuronal DCP1 in a cell non-autonomous mechanism that uses neuronally derived signals to orchestrate wing disc development.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the tissue-specific knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Abnormal wing discs and malformed adult wings appeared with a similar frequency of 50–60% in elav:GAL4 >UAS:IRDCP1 flies grown at 25°C.
claims.source: Interestingly, abnormal wing discs and malformed adult wings appeared with a similar frequency of 50–60% in elav:GAL4 >UAS:IRDCP1 flies grown at 25°C, suggesting a cause-and-effect relationship between them.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological observations.

claims.claim: Restricting neuronal DCP1 knockdown to embryonic and larval stages leads to the formation of abnormal wing discs but does not affect the phenotype of adult wings.
claims.source: Switching between DCP1-ON and OFF states at different developmental stages (Figure 7) revealed that restricting neuronal knockdown in embryonic and larval stages leads to the formation of abnormal wing discs (five out of nine examined wing imaginal discs displayed abnormalities in tissue folding and F-actin accumulation) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) but does not affect the phenotype of adult wings.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Starting neuronal DCP1 knockdown from the white pupa stage is sufficient for causing malformed wings.
claims.source: Congruently, starting knockdown from the white pupa stage, when wing discs are already formed is sufficient for causing malformed wings.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Abnormalities in wing imaginal discs tissue pattern and aberrant adult wing morphology represent two unconnected outcomes of neuronal DCP1 deficiency, which occur independently at different developmental stages.
claims.source: Therefore, abnormalities in wing imaginal discs tissue pattern and aberrant adult wing morphology represent two unconnected outcomes of neuronal DCP1 deficiency, which occur independently at different developmental stages.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temperature-shift experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The crucial period where neuronal DCP1 activity impacts adult wing development is between the white pupa and the 3-day pupa stages.
claims.source: Taking into account, the potential latency between any temperature shift and the subsequent effect in gene expression, we can safely place the crucial period where neuronal DCP1 activity impacts adult wing development between the white pupa and the 3-day pupa stages.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temperature-shift experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Neuronal activity of DCAP-1/DCP1 participates in the inter-tissue crosstalk that regulates ageing through neurosecretion.
claims.source: In this study, we have shown that neuronal activity of DCAP-1/DCP1, which is the regulatory subunit of the core mRNA decapping enzyme, participates in the inter-tissue crosstalk that regulates ageing through neurosecretion.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the combined experimental data from C. elegans presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Neuronal overexpression of dcap-1 is sufficient to extend nematode lifespan, in a DCAP-2-dependent manner, regardless of DCAP-1 availability in other tissues.
claims.source: Using appropriate strains designed to express DCAP-1::GFP fusion protein in a tissue-selective manner, we found that neuronal overexpression is sufficient to extend nematode lifespan, in a DCAP-2-dependent manner, regardless of DCAP-1 availability in other tissues.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The effect of neuronal dcap-1 overexpression on lifespan is exerted through the action of IIS and the downstream transcription factor DAF-16/FOXO.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that the effect of neuronal dcap-1 overexpression on lifespan is exerted through the action of IIS and the downstream transcription factor DAF-16/FOXO.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: DCAP-1 activity in the nervous system controls the expression levels of ins-7 gene, encoding an insulin-like peptide that is upregulated during ageing and acts as a DAF-2/InsR agonist.
claims.source: More specifically, DCAP-1 activity in the nervous system controls the expression levels of ins-7 gene, encoding an insulin-like peptide that is upregulated during ageing and acts as a DAF-2/InsR agonist.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and reporter data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Short-lived dcap-1 mutant adults show higher mRNA levels of ins-7, compared to wt animals.
claims.source: We found that short-lived dcap-1 mutant adults show higher mRNA levels of ins-7, compared to wt animals, whereas dcap-1 overexpression in neurons, significantly hampers the age-dependent mRNA upsurge of ins-7.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: dcap-1 overexpression in neurons significantly hampers the age-dependent mRNA upsurge of ins-7.
claims.source: We found that short-lived dcap-1 mutant adults show higher mRNA levels of ins-7, compared to wt animals, whereas dcap-1 overexpression in neurons, significantly hampers the age-dependent mRNA upsurge of ins-7.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Elevated ins-7 mRNA levels in dcap-1 mutants coincide with increased transcription of ins-7 in their intestine.
claims.source: Elevated ins-7 mRNA levels in dcap-1 mutants coincide with increased transcription of ins-7 in their intestine, despite the fact that ins-7 is predominantly expressed in neurons (Pierce et al., 2001; Murphy et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ins-7p::gfp reporter data shown in Figure 3B and citations to Pierce et al., 2001 and Murphy et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Overexpression of neuronal dcap-1 extends lifespan through IIS intertissue signaling initiated by lower levels of neuronal INS-7.
claims.source: Overall, our data strongly implied the involvement of a neuroendocrine mechanism leading to the hypothesis that overexpression of neuronal dcap-1 extends lifespan through IIS intertissue signaling initiated by lower levels of neuronal INS-7.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Post-transcriptional stabilization of neuronal ins-7 mRNA occurs in decapping mutants.
claims.source: This hypothesis is supported by the following evidence: a) We demonstrated post-transcriptional stabilization of neuronal ins-7 mRNA in decapping mutants, b) deletion of ins-7 gene suppresses the induction of ins-7p::gfp in the intestine of dcap-1 mutants, in a similar way to unc-31/CAPS mutants, where neuropeptide secretion is strongly inhibited, c) ins-7 RNAi in a neuronal RNAi-sensitive background increases lifespan of wt animals but fails to further extend the already long life of worms overexpressing neuronal dcap-1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Deletion of ins-7 gene suppresses the induction of ins-7p::gfp in the intestine of dcap-1 mutants, in a similar way to unc-31/CAPS mutants, where neuropeptide secretion is strongly inhibited.
claims.source: This hypothesis is supported by the following evidence: a) We demonstrated post-transcriptional stabilization of neuronal ins-7 mRNA in decapping mutants, b) deletion of ins-7 gene suppresses the induction of ins-7p::gfp in the intestine of dcap-1 mutants, in a similar way to unc-31/CAPS mutants, where neuropeptide secretion is strongly inhibited, c) ins-7 RNAi in a neuronal RNAi-sensitive background increases lifespan of wt animals but fails to further extend the already long life of worms overexpressing neuronal dcap-1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figures 3C and 3F.

claims.claim: Lower neurosecretion of INS-7 in dcap-1 overexpressing animals could subsequently reduce IIS and activate DAF-16 in intestinal cells, ultimately downregulating the expression of intestinal ins-7.
claims.source: Lower neurosecretion of this DAF-2 agonist in dcap-1 overexpressing animals could subsequently reduce IIS and activate DAF-16 in intestinal cells, ultimately downregulating the expression of intestinal ins-7.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and known biology of IIS.

claims.claim: Translocation of DAF-16 to the nucleus is delayed in all tissues of dcap-1 worms, during normal conditions and the early stages of heat-shock.
claims.source: Indeed, we monitored that translocation of DAF-16 to the nucleus, is delayed in all tissues of dcap-1 worms, during normal conditions and the early stages of heat-shock, while overexpression of neuronal dcap-1 enhanced the localization of DAF-16 in both cases.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of neuronal dcap-1 enhanced the localization of DAF-16 to the nucleus during normal conditions and the early stages of heat-shock.
claims.source: Indeed, we monitored that translocation of DAF-16 to the nucleus, is delayed in all tissues of dcap-1 worms, during normal conditions and the early stages of heat-shock, while overexpression of neuronal dcap-1 enhanced the localization of DAF-16 in both cases.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The longevity effect of neuronal dcap-1 overexpression correlated with increased stress resistance in mid-aged animals, but not in young adults.
claims.source: Oddly, the longevity effect of neuronal dcap-1 overexpression correlated with increased stress resistance in mid-aged animals, but not in young adults.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by stress resistance data shown in Figures 4C-F.

claims.claim: The difference in stress resistance between young and aged animals probably reflects the greater need of ageing worms for protective mechanisms toward accumulating stress factors.
claims.source: This difference probably reflects the greater need of ageing worms for protective mechanisms toward accumulating stress factors (Walther et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference and is supported by a citation to Walther et al., 2015.

claims.claim: DAF-16 translocates to the nucleus of aged animals in order to stabilize their transcriptome, as a response to age-associated cellular stress.
claims.source: DAF-16 was recently reported to translocate to the nucleus of aged animals in order to stabilize their transcriptome, as a response to age-associated cellular stress (Li et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Deficiency of decapping enhancer EDC-3 extends lifespan in C. elegans by suppressing protein synthesis in neurons, due to sequestration of translation factors into P-bodies, which then triggers stress response through multiple longevity effectors.
claims.source: A thought-provoking study reported that deficiency of decapping enhancer EDC-3 extends lifespan in C. elegans by suppressing protein synthesis in neurons, due to sequestration of translation factors into P-bodies, which then triggers stress response through multiple longevity effectors (Rieckher et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rieckher et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The contrasting effect of DCAP-1 and EDC-3 on lifespan is in line with the role of decapping activators that function to provide specificity toward diverse mRNA substrates through particular interactions with them or with other decapping enhancers.
claims.source: Although counterintuitive, this contrasting effect of DCAP-1 and EDC-3 on lifespan is in line with the role of decapping activators that function to provide specificity toward diverse mRNA substrates through particular interactions with them or with other decapping enhancers (He et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference and is supported by a citation to He et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The mechanism by which neuronal overexpression of dcap-1 extends lifespan is completely dependent on DCAP-2 activity.
claims.source: Moreover, the mechanism by which neuronal overexpression of dcap-1 extends lifespan is completely dependent on DCAP-2 activity, and cannot be attributed to secondary effects emerging from the increased P-body formation that is evident in both wt and dcap-2 backgrounds (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2E and referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Regulation of ageing via neurons appears to be conserved in D. melanogaster.
claims.source: The fact that regulation of ageing via neurons appears to be conserved in D. melanogaster (Tatar et al., 2001; Libert et al., 2007), combined with the strong evolutionary conservation of the 5'−3' mRNA decay prompted us to investigate the connection between neuronal decapping and ageing in the fruit fly.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tatar et al., 2001 and Libert et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Neuron-specific knockdown of DCP1 in D. melanogaster greatly reduces lifespan.
claims.source: We showed that neuron-specific knockdown of the fly dcap-1 orthologue DCP1 greatly reduces lifespan, while its neuronal overexpression leads to a significant induction of longevity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Neuronal overexpression of DCP1 in D. melanogaster leads to a significant induction of longevity.
claims.source: We showed that neuron-specific knockdown of the fly dcap-1 orthologue DCP1 greatly reduces lifespan, while its neuronal overexpression leads to a significant induction of longevity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Neuronal overexpression of DCP1 in D. melanogaster leads to longevity only when overexpression occurs post-developmentally.
claims.source: The latter though applies only when overexpression occurs post-developmentally.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The fly genome encodes eight insulin-like peptides (DILP1-8), four of which are expressed in neurons and are linked with lifespan regulation.
claims.source: The fly genome encodes eight insulin-like peptides (DILP1-8), four of which are expressed in neurons and are linked with lifespan regulation (Kannan and Fridell, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kannan and Fridell, 2013.

claims.claim: The exoribonuclease Pacman/XRN1 has been reported to regulate the levels of secreted molecules in D. melanogaster, including insulin-like peptide DIPL8 and neuropeptide NPLP2.
claims.source: Moreover, the exoribonuclease Pacman/XRN1, which acts downstream of decapping in the 5'−3' mRNA decay pathway, has been reported to regulate the levels of secreted molecules in D. melanogaster, including insulin-like peptide DIPL8 and neuropeptide NPLP2 (Jones et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2016.

claims.claim: mRNA decapping may play an active and extended role in the control of neurosecretion in the fly.
claims.source: This indicates that mRNA decapping may play an active and extended role in the control of neurosecretion in the fly.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited work on Pacman/XRN1.

claims.claim: All morphological traits of neuronal DCP1-deficient flies are connected with processes that take place in newly eclosed adults, during the late phases of the last ecdysis.
claims.source: Of note, all morphological traits of neuronal DCP1-deficient flies are connected with processes that take place in newly eclosed adults, during the late phases of the last ecdysis.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the morphological observations.

claims.claim: Release of neuropeptide bursicon from neurons of the subesophageal and abdominal ganglia orchestrates the execution of a posteclosion program, characterized by a combination of behavioral and anatomical changes that act in concert and ultimately lead to wing expansion and cuticle tanning.
claims.source: At this stage, release of neuropeptide bursicon (also known as the tanning hormone) from neurons of the subesophageal and abdominal ganglia orchestrates the execution of a posteclosion program, characterized by a combination of behavioral and anatomical changes that act in concert and ultimately lead to wing expansion and cuticle tanning (Peabody et al., 2008; White and Ewer, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peabody et al., 2008 and White and Ewer, 2014.

claims.claim: rickets, the bursicon receptor, functions in a set of insulin-like peptide ILP7-secreting peptidergic neurons of the ventral nervous system to regulate the tanning of Drosophila adult cuticle.
claims.source: A recent study revealed that rickets, the bursicon receptor, functions in a set of insulin-like peptide ILP7-secreting peptidergic neurons of the ventral nervous system to regulate the tanning of Drosophila adult cuticle (Flaven-Pouchon et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Flaven-Pouchon et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Mutants defective for bursicon or rickets fail to induce both behavioral and anatomical aspects of the posteclosion program and consequently form adults with unexpanded wings, unexpanded thorax and untanned cuticle.
claims.source: Mutants defective for bursicon or rickets, fail to induce both behavioral and anatomical aspects of this program and consequently form adults with unexpanded wings, unexpanded thorax and untanned cuticle (Dewey et al., 2004; Baker and Truman, 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dewey et al., 2004 and Baker and Truman, 2002.

claims.claim: The striking similarity between neuronal DCP1 knockdown flies and bursicon/rickets mutants strongly suggests that flies subjected to neuronal DCP1 knockdown exhibit some kind of impairment in bursicon signaling.
claims.source: The striking similarity to these mutants strongly suggests that flies subjected to neuronal DCP1 knockdown exhibit some kind of impairment in bursicon signaling.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the morphological similarities.

claims.claim: Initial measurements show a trend for lower bursicon and rickets mRNA levels in heads dissected from newly eclosed adults when neuronal DCP1 is knocked-down.
claims.source: In favor of this notion, our initial measurements show a trend for lower bursicon and rickets mRNA levels in heads dissected from newly eclosed adults when neuronal DCP1 is knocked-down (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data referenced in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: DCP1 knockdown at the last ecdysis does not affect wing expansion.
claims.source: However, our data cannot support a direct connection between DCP1 levels and bursicon activity during the last ecdysis, since DCP1 knockdown at that point does not affect wing expansion.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Neuronal DCP1 activity during earlier stages of pupal development is essential for the function of an intermediate factor, which subsequently affects bursicon signaling and hence the corresponding posteclosion program.
claims.source: It is rather more likely that neuronal DCP1 activity during earlier stages of pupal development is essential for the function of an intermediate factor, which subsequently affects bursicon signaling and hence the corresponding posteclosion program.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the temperature-shift experiments.

claims.claim: A similar mechanism could affect the morphology of wing imaginal discs during neuronal DCP1 knockdown, as bursicon expression is also detected during early larval development.
claims.source: A similar mechanism could affect the morphology of wing imaginal discs during neuronal DCP1 knockdown, as bursicon expression is also detected during early larval development (Honegger et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation and is supported by a citation to Honegger et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The decapping enzyme and its regulators have been implicated in the control of local translation at the synapse, synaptic plasticity and related modifications of neuronal activity in Drosophila and mammals.
claims.source: This is in line with previous work that has implicated the decapping enzyme and its regulators in the control of local translation at the synapse, synaptic plasticity and related modifications of neuronal activity in Drosophila and mammals (Barbee et al., 2006; Hillebrand et al., 2010; Zeitelhofer et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barbee et al., 2006, Hillebrand et al., 2010, and Zeitelhofer et al., 2008.

claims.claim: mRNA decapping factors should no longer be considered as mere housekeeping genes that serve in the indiscriminate degradation of mRNA molecules, but as actual gene expression regulators that have active roles in the control of neuronal function.
claims.source: Taken together, such findings reestablish our understanding concerning mRNA decapping factors which should no longer be considered as mere housekeeping genes that serve in the indiscriminate degradation of mRNA molecules, but as actual gene expression regulators that have active roles in the control of neuronal function.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined findings of this study and previous work.

results.result: Neuronal expression of dcap-1 rescues the short lifespan of dcap-1 mutants in C. elegans. Tissue-specific rescue experiments show that neuronal dcap-1 expression fully restores lifespan to wild-type levels at both 20°C and 25°C, while expression in epidermis or muscles has minimal effect, and intestinal expression shows intermediate rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C47 are well-supported by lifespan data in Figure 1 showing tissue-specific rescue experiments. The neuronal rescue is robust and reproducible with two different promoters (unc-119p and rab-3p), while other tissues show minimal or intermediate effects. The data clearly demonstrate tissue-specific requirements for dcap-1 in lifespan regulation.

results.result: Neuronal overexpression of dcap-1 extends lifespan in wild-type C. elegans in a decapping-dependent manner. Neuronal dcap-1 overexpression increases median lifespan by ~13-16% and maximum lifespan by ~18-26%, accompanied by delayed age-dependent movement decline. The effect requires DCAP-2 catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 and C54 are strongly supported by lifespan data in Figure 2A-E showing consistent lifespan extension with neuronal dcap-1 overexpression using multiple promoters. The requirement for DCAP-2 (C54) demonstrates specificity for the decapping mechanism. The movement data (C52) provides functional validation of healthspan extension.

results.result: Neuronal dcap-1-mediated lifespan extension requires DAF-16/FOXO and acts through insulin/IGF-like signaling (IIS). Genetic epistasis experiments show that daf-16 mutation or knockdown abolishes the longevity effect of neuronal dcap-1 overexpression, and daf-2 knockdown masks the effect, indicating dcap-1 acts upstream of or through IIS.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59, C62-C63 are well-supported by genetic epistasis data in Figure 2F-H. The lack of additive effects with daf-16 mutation and daf-2 RNAi, combined with the epistasis analysis, provide strong evidence for dcap-1 acting through the IIS pathway. The logic of the epistasis experiments is sound.

results.result: DCAP-1 regulates ins-7 mRNA levels in an age-dependent manner. dcap-1 mutants show elevated ins-7 mRNA (doubled in young adults, seven-fold increase with age), while neuronal dcap-1 overexpression suppresses age-dependent ins-7 upregulation. Other insulin-like peptides (daf-28, ins-33, ins-1, ins-6) are unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68, C71, C121-C122 are supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3A showing specific regulation of ins-7 but not other ILPs. The age-dependent changes are quantified and statistically significant. The specificity for ins-7 strengthens the conclusion that this is not a general effect on ILP expression.

results.result: Elevated ins-7 mRNA in dcap-1 mutants reflects increased transcription specifically in the intestine. ins-7p::gfp reporter fluorescence is 1.6-2.1-fold higher in dcap-1 mutants across all ages, with the increase restricted to intestinal cells. A control ges-1p::gfp reporter shows no increase in dcap-1 background.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75, C123 are supported by fluorescence reporter data in Figure 3B and supplements. The tissue-specific increase in intestinal but not neuronal ins-7p::gfp expression, combined with the negative control (ges-1p::gfp), provides strong evidence for transcriptional regulation in the intestine. The quantification is appropriate.

results.result: Neuronal DCAP-1 regulates intestinal ins-7 expression through dense core vesicle (DCV) neurosecretion. unc-31/CAPS mutation (blocking DCV release) eliminates ins-7p::gfp differences between dcap-1 and wild-type, while unc-13 mutation (blocking small clear vesicles) does not. Neuronal dcap-1 restoration normalizes ins-7 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C79, C81-C83, C126 are well-supported by experiments with neurosecretion mutants in Figure 3C-E. The differential effects of unc-31 vs unc-13 mutations provide mechanistic insight into the neurosecretion pathway involved. The tissue-specific rescue experiments (C81-C82) further support the neuronal origin of the signal.

results.result: DCAP-1 regulates ins-7 through post-transcriptional stabilization of neuronal ins-7 mRNA. ins-7 deletion suppresses ins-7p::gfp induction in dcap-1 mutants. Using a neuronal unc-119p::ins-7 transgene, mature ins-7 mRNA shows two-fold elevation in dcap-1 mutants, which is specific (not seen with reference gene eft-3).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86, C125 are supported by genetic and molecular data in Figure 3F-G and supplements. The ins-7 deletion experiment (C84) demonstrates ins-7 is required for the phenotype. The mature/pre-mRNA ratio analysis (C85-C86) provides direct evidence for post-transcriptional regulation, with appropriate controls showing specificity.

results.result: Low INS-7 levels mediate lifespan extension from neuronal dcap-1 overexpression. ins-7 RNAi extends wild-type lifespan but fails to further extend lifespan in neuronal dcap-1 overexpressing animals, indicating lack of additivity and suggesting dcap-1 acts through ins-7 regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89, C124 are supported by genetic epistasis data in Figure 3H. The lack of additive effect between ins-7 RNAi and neuronal dcap-1 overexpression is consistent with dcap-1 acting through ins-7. However, the inference (C89, C124) is somewhat indirect and could benefit from additional mechanistic validation.

results.result: DCAP-1 regulates DAF-16 nuclear translocation. dcap-1 depletion delays DAF-16::GFP nuclear translocation under normal conditions and during early heat shock, while neuronal dcap-1 overexpression enhances DAF-16a::RFP nuclear localization even without stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92, C128-C129 are supported by microscopy data in Figure 4A-B and supplements showing DAF-16 localization. The quantification of nuclear-localized DAF-16 is appropriate. However, the use of different fluorophores (GFP vs RFP) in different experiments makes direct comparison challenging, as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: Neuronal dcap-1 overexpression provides age-dependent stress resistance. Young adults (1 day) show no enhanced resistance to heat shock or oxidative stress, but aged animals (3+ days for oxidative stress, 9 days for heat shock) show significantly increased stress resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97, C130 are supported by stress resistance assays in Figure 4C-F. The age-dependent effect is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls. The interpretation (C97) that this reflects slower aging is reasonable but somewhat speculative, as alternative explanations (e.g., age-specific protective mechanisms) are possible.

results.result: Neuron-specific knockdown of DCP1 in D. melanogaster significantly reduces lifespan. elav:GAL4-driven DCP1 RNAi results in extremely short-lived flies at both 25°C and 29°C compared to parental controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C100, C137 are supported by lifespan data in Figure 5B-C showing dramatic lifespan reduction with neuronal DCP1 knockdown. The effect is verified by qRT-PCR (Figure 5A) and is consistent across two independent RNAi lines, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Post-developmental neuronal DCP1 overexpression extends lifespan in D. melanogaster. Constitutive neuronal DCP1 overexpression does not extend lifespan, but post-developmental overexpression (using GAL80ts) increases median lifespan by ~42% and maximum by ~27%, indicating developmental stage-specific effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103, C138-C139 are supported by lifespan data in Figure 5D and source data. The temperature-shift experiment using GAL80ts is well-designed to separate developmental from adult effects. The contrasting results between developmental and post-developmental overexpression provide important mechanistic insight.

results.result: Neuronal DCP1 knockdown causes wing and cuticle developmental defects in D. melanogaster. ~50% of flies at 25°C (95% at 29°C) show malformed/unexpanded wings, unexpanded thorax, and lack of cuticle tanning, indicating cell non-autonomous effects of neuronal DCP1 on development.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 are supported by morphological observations in Figure 5E-F. The high penetrance and consistent co-occurrence of multiple phenotypes strengthen the conclusion. The inference of cell non-autonomous effects (C107) is reasonable given the neuronal-specific knockdown affects non-neuronal tissues.

results.result: Neuronal DCP1 affects wing imaginal disc development through cell non-autonomous mechanisms. 15/23 wing discs from neuronal DCP1 knockdown larvae show structural abnormalities. elav:GAL4-driven GFP is absent from wing discs, and en:GAL4-driven DCP1 knockdown in posterior disc cells does not cause abnormalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by microscopy data in Figure 6A-C. The control experiments (C109-C110) effectively rule out cell-autonomous effects and leaky expression, strengthening the conclusion of cell non-autonomous signaling. The frequency of abnormal discs (15/23) is substantial.

results.result: Wing disc and adult wing defects from neuronal DCP1 knockdown are temporally separable. Temperature-shift experiments show that larval-stage knockdown causes disc abnormalities but not adult wing defects, while knockdown from white pupa stage causes wing malformations. The critical period for adult wing development is between white pupa and 3-day pupa stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 are supported by temperature-shift experiments in Figure 7. The temporal dissection is well-designed and provides important mechanistic insight. The inference about the critical period (C116) appropriately accounts for potential latency in gene expression changes.

results.result: DCAP-1/DCP1 has a conserved function in developmental events and lifespan modulation across C. elegans and D. melanogaster. The findings establish mRNA decapping factors as gene expression regulators with active roles in neuronal function, rather than mere housekeeping genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C117, C153 represent the overarching conclusions supported by the combined data from both organisms. The conservation of neuronal DCP1 effects on lifespan and development across species is well-demonstrated. The conceptual reframing (C153) is justified by the data, though somewhat interpretive.

results.result: Neuronal DCAP-1 acts cell non-autonomously through signals that influence DAF-16 in distal tissues. Lower INS-7 neurosecretion in dcap-1 overexpressing animals reduces IIS and activates DAF-16 in intestinal cells, downregulating intestinal ins-7 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C61, C127 represent mechanistic inferences supported by multiple lines of evidence (neurosecretion experiments, tissue-specific effects, DAF-16 localization). The proposed model is consistent with the data, though some aspects remain indirect. The cell non-autonomous nature is well-established.

results.result: Neuronal DCP1 knockdown phenotypes in D. melanogaster resemble bursicon/rickets mutants, suggesting impaired bursicon signaling. Preliminary qRT-PCR shows trends for lower bursicon and rickets mRNA. However, DCP1 knockdown at eclosion does not affect wing expansion, suggesting DCP1 acts on an intermediate factor during earlier pupal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 involve mechanistic speculation about bursicon signaling. While the phenotypic similarity (C147) is striking, the molecular evidence is preliminary (C148 shows only trends, not significant differences). The temporal analysis (C149-C150) provides some support but the mechanism remains unclear. Additional validation is needed.

results.result: Background and context claims about mRNA decapping, P-bodies, IIS pathway, and prior work on dcap-1/DCP1. These establish the scientific foundation and cite relevant literature on mRNA cap homeostasis, decapping mechanisms, neurological importance, and the IIS pathway in aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C38 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide necessary context but do not represent novel findings of this study. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made.

results.result: Additional background claims citing prior work on dcap-1 rescue, aging markers, IIS components, neurosecretion machinery, stress-aging links, DCP1 lethality, bursicon signaling, and synaptic functions of decapping. These provide methodological validation and mechanistic context.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C53, C60, C64-C65, C69-C70, C76, C78, C80, C87, C90, C98-C99, C131-C134, C136, C140-C141, C144-C146, C152 are supported by appropriate citations. These establish prior knowledge and methodological foundations but are not novel findings of this manuscript.

results.result: Summary claims from abstract and introduction stating the main findings. These synthesize the detailed results about neuronal dcap-1/DCP1 effects on lifespan, INS-7 regulation, DAF-16 localization, and conservation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C9, C39-C40, C118-C120 are high-level summaries of the main findings, supported by the detailed experimental data discussed in other result groups. These represent accurate summaries of the work, though they are redundant with more specific claims.

results.result: Mechanistic interpretations and speculations. The lifespan extension mechanism depends on DCAP-2 and cannot be attributed to P-body formation. mRNA decapping may have extended roles in neurosecretion control. Bursicon expression in larvae might explain wing disc phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 is well-supported by data in Figure 2E. Claims C142 and C151 are more speculative inferences based on indirect evidence (C142 from XRN1 data, C151 from developmental expression patterns). These represent reasonable hypotheses but would benefit from direct testing.
